newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW - Xoma hopeful after E5 setback.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Xoma hopeful after E5 setback.

text.p: Xoma Corp, which recently discontinued U.S. trials of its E5 monoclonal antibody to treat sepsis, is still hopeful that the product will be approved in Japan, Chairman Jack Castello said on Friday.

In an interview, Castello said the company faced a lighter burden of proof in Japan in demonstrating the efficacy of the product. He said it already passed through five of the six steps in the drug-approval process there. The product failed to produce statistically significant positive results in U.S. trials,
If E5 were approved in Japan, it could generate up to $25 million in annual revenues, Castello said.

"The value to Xoma of an approval of E5 in Japan is between half and the full cost of running this company," he said, adding that Xoma's annual cash needs are about $25 million. Castello said he expected the Japanese approval processs to last about another year.

Castello also said preliminary results of its hu11 24 monoclonal antibody for psoriasis "look promising," despite the problem of flu-like side effects, including fever and nausea, that forced the company to adjust dosing levels. Xoma will cut the test dose to one-tenth its original size to see if potency can be achieved without severe side effects.

The company, however, is putting most of its resources into its Neuprex drug candidate, designed to treat a range of serious infections, including meningococcemia, a bacterial disease that strikes children and can lead to death within hours.
Castello said Xoma was ahead of schedule in its Phase III trials of Neuprex as a treatment for meningococcemia and should complete testing by end of 1998, if not earlier.

It also plans to start a pivotal Phase III trial by June or July to test Neuprex as a treatment for hemorrhagic trauma, associated with severe blood loss often seen in victims of car accidents or gunshot wounds. That trial is expected to last between one and two years.

While Neuprex has been most widely recognized as a potential treatment for the deadly children's infection, Castello said the market for treating hemorrhagic trauma could be much larger, worth an estimated $200 million to $300 million a year in U.S. and Europe. He estimated the size of the meningococcemia market at $10 million to $15 million a year.
